solver.kind: blind AI solver B (separate agent, answer-free packet, adversarial rubric)

R063-01.notes: A contradicted by the agents study; C contradicted by para 4 (warnings did little); D misattributes the discovery (T&K came first, and agents were subjects, not researchers). B covers both halves of the passage: irrelevant anchors (paras 1-2) and changing the starting point (para 5).

R063-02.notes: Direct detail: the 65 group's median was 45. B (25) is the 10 group's median, a swap trap; A and C are the anchor values themselves. Fact check: medians of 25 and 45 match Tversky & Kahneman (1974).

R063-03.notes: Supported by para 2: the anchor 'need not be relevant ... need not be believed.' B is the reverse of 'everyone could see'; C goes against the point that the number was random; D is not supported (no true value is given). Fact check: the wheel being rigged to 10 or 65 matches Kahneman's later account (Thinking, Fast and Slow); the 1974 paper says only that the wheel was spun in front of subjects. This simplification is accurate enough, not a flag.

R063-04.notes: Appraisals tracked the listing price, yet few mentioned it. A ('deliberately') is the strongest distractor, but 'few mentioned' undercuts deliberate use. B is the opposite of the 'however' turn; D has no support. Fact check: this matches Northcraft & Neale (1987), where agents toured a house, the packet listing price was varied, and agents seldom cited the price as a factor.

R063-05.notes: 'So crude an influence' means a simple, unsophisticated influence that experts should see through. A is the literal sense (crude oil); C is the 'crude joke' sense; D ('crude estimate') is the strongest alternate, but an influence is not 'approximate'. Ordinary ACT vocabulary-in-context item.

R063-06.notes: Close paraphrase of para 4. A is related to the agents' lack of awareness, but the passage frames it as not noticing, not refusing; B contradicts 'need not be believed'; C overstates (the passage says warnings did little, not that they made things worse).

R063-07.notes: Matches 'generate their own estimate before seeing any number.' B is a warning, which the passage says did little. C and D still involve the anchor, and the expertise study shows experts do not escape it. Fact check: consider-the-opposite (Mussweiler, Strack & Pfeiffer 2000) and limited warning effects (Wilson et al. 1996) are accurately stated. The self-generated-estimate remedy is simplified but defensible.

R063-08.notes: Para 4 explains the mechanism (it works before deliberate reasoning, and correction stops too soon) and why warnings fail. A is para 3; B is para 5; D is explicitly rejected ('not because people are careless').

R063-09.notes: Directly stated: 'a listing price, which the researchers varied.' The other choices have no support. Fact check: matches Northcraft & Neale (1987).

R063-10.notes: 'Remedy ... lies less in trying harder,' and correction starts from the anchor, so the author is skeptical. D is the strongest trap, but the passage says effort is insufficient, not that it makes the bias worse. A contradicts the passage; C is false because effort is discussed. The reasons attached to each attitude make the item clean.
